sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and Athletic Performance
sources.author: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM (Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, American College of Sports Medicine)
sources.trust_reason: Joint position of three professional bodies, published concurrently in Med Sci Sports Exerc 48(3):543-568 and J Acad Nutr Diet 116(3):501-528.
sources.notes: Sets out energy, macronutrient, fluid and supplement guidance for athletes across training and competition, and recommends individualized advice from a sports dietitian.
sources.population_note: Full text paywalled; abstract silent on sex, but secondary sources citing it confirm female-relevant guidance (iron screening for women with heavy menstruation, low energy availability/Triad); evidence base not split by sex. Rating based on secondary sources; full text not reviewed.

sources.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: nutrient timing
sources.author: Kerksick CM, Arent S, Schoenfeld BJ, et al. (ISSN)
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed society position stand in J Int Soc Sports Nutr 14:33.
sources.notes: Reviews when to eat carbohydrate and protein around training and how timing affects glycogen, recovery and adaptation.
sources.population_note: Authors state most nutrient-timing studies evaluated men and carb guidance rests on male endurance athletes; notes women oxidize more fat and may need more total energy when carb loading.

sources.title: International society of sports nutrition position stand: caffeine and exercise performance
sources.author: Guest NS, VanDusseldorp TA, Nelson MT, et al. (ISSN)
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed society position stand in J Int Soc Sports Nutr (doi 10.1186/s12970-020-00383-4).
sources.notes: Summarizes evidence on caffeine dose, timing, forms and side effects for endurance and other exercise.
sources.population_note: Cites several mixed-sex and female-only trials; concludes endurance benefits do not appear to differ by sex; notes hormonal contraceptives and pregnancy slow caffeine metabolism; no menstrual-cycle analysis.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement
sources.author: Sawka MN, Burke LM, Eichner ER, Maughan RJ, Montain SJ, Stachenfeld NS (ACSM)
sources.trust_reason: ACSM official position stand, Med Sci Sports Exerc 39(2):377-390.
sources.notes: Covers hydrating before, during and after exercise, estimating sweat rate from body weight, and electrolyte needs.
sources.population_note: Abstract frames sweat variability as individual, not by sex; full text paywalled and could not be checked for sex-specific content.

sources.title: 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs)
sources.author: Mountjoy M, Ackerman KE, Bailey DM, et al. (IOC)
sources.trust_reason: IOC expert consensus published in Br J Sports Med 57(17):1073-1097.
sources.notes: Describes low energy availability as a spectrum, its health and performance effects, and the REDs CAT2 screening and risk tool.
sources.population_note: REDs grew out of the Female Athlete Triad; assessment tool uses female indicators (menstrual function, amenorrhoea) and separate male ones (testosterone); abstract notes male data still emerging.

sources.title: IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete
sources.author: Maughan RJ, Burke LM, Dvorak J, et al. (IOC)
sources.trust_reason: IOC expert consensus published in Br J Sports Med 52(7):439-455 (CC BY-NC).
sources.notes: Weighs evidence for performance supplements such as caffeine, nitrate and bicarbonate, plus contamination and anti-doping risk.
sources.population_note: Gives sex-specific iron intake thresholds (above 18 mg/day women, 8 mg/day men), flags menstrual blood loss and menstrual dysfunction for iron and calcium/vitamin D; no sex analysis of ergogenic effects.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.author: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Fiatarone Singh MA, et al.; Phillips SM (ACSM)
sources.trust_reason: ACSM position stand in Med Sci Sports Exerc 58(4), an overview of 137 systematic reviews (CC BY-NC-ND); replaces the 2009 progression-models stand.
sources.notes: Gives evidence-based ranges for load, sets, frequency and progression of strength training in healthy adults.
sources.population_note: Overview of 137 systematic reviews with over 30,000 adults; no sex breakdown and no sex-specific recommendations, though some included reviews are women-only.

sources.title: How much is too much? (Part 1) International Olympic Committee consensus statement on load in sport and risk of injury
sources.author: Soligard T, Schwellnus M, Alonso JM, et al. (IOC)
sources.trust_reason: IOC expert consensus published in Br J Sports Med 50(17):1030-1041.
sources.notes: Links rapid load changes and poor load management to injury and gives guidance on prescribing and monitoring training load.
sources.population_note: Abstract and indexing give no detail on sex; full text paywalled and not checked.

sources.title: Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia: 2019 Update
sources.author: Bennett BL, Hew-Butler T, Rosner MH, Myers T, Lipman GS (Wilderness Medical Society)
sources.trust_reason: Society clinical practice guideline in Wilderness Environ Med 31(1):50-62.
sources.notes: Identifies fluid overconsumption as the main cause of exercise-associated hyponatremia and favors drinking to thirst for prevention.
sources.population_note: Abstract silent on sex; secondary summaries of its risk-factor table list BMI, slow pace and overdrinking but not female sex; full text paywalled.

sources.title: ACSM Expert Consensus Statement on Exertional Heat Illness: Recognition, Management, and Return to Activity
sources.author: Roberts WO, Armstrong LE, Sawka MN, Yeargin SW, Heled Y, O'Connor FG (ACSM)
sources.trust_reason: ACSM expert consensus in Curr Sports Med Rep 22(4), the replacement version of the 2021 statement.
sources.notes: Covers recognizing heat exhaustion and heat stroke, rapid whole-body cooling, prevention and return to running; note a published dissent letter on some points.
sources.population_note: Lists NCAA heat-illness rates for men's and women's sports and cites a review of sex differences, but gives no sex-specific recognition, cooling or return-to-play guidance.

sources.title: A step towards personalized sports nutrition: carbohydrate intake during exercise
sources.author: Jeukendrup A
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed review in Sports Medicine 44(Suppl 1) by a leading researcher on exercise carbohydrate metabolism.
sources.notes: Explains how carbohydrate intake during exercise should scale with event duration and the role of multiple transportable sugars.
sources.population_note: Narrative review; cites one Ironman study where women took about 1.0 and men 1.1 g/kg/h carb, with the intake-performance link not seen in women; otherwise no sex analysis.

sources.title: Effects of Strength Training on the Physiological Determinants of Middle- and Long-Distance Running Performance: A Systematic Review
sources.author: Blagrove RC, Howatson G, Hayes PR
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed systematic review in Sports Medicine 48(5).
sources.notes: Finds that adding strength and plyometric work tends to improve running economy in distance runners without harming aerobic fitness.
sources.population_note: 24 studies, 469 runners: 352 male and 96 female (about 79% male); only two female-only studies; authors list female runners as an under-researched group.

sources.title: Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.author: Wang Z, Wang YT, Gao W, Zhong Y
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed systematic review and meta-analysis in PLoS One (doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0282838).
sources.notes: Pools taper studies in endurance athletes to compare taper length, volume reduction and intensity on performance.
sources.population_note: 14 studies, 174 athletes; only 7 women (about 4%) across two studies; no sex subgroup; authors note results may not represent female athletes.

sources.title: Regulation of Muscle Glycogen Metabolism during Exercise: Implications for Endurance Performance and Training Adaptations
sources.author: Hearris MA, Hammond KM, Fell JM, Morton JP
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed review in Nutrients 10(3):298 from an academic sports nutrition group.
sources.notes: Explains how glycogen stores govern endurance capacity and how pre-race carbohydrate loading and training-low strategies relate to them.
sources.population_note: Key glycogen figure compiled from males only and most cited trials used men; authors mention gender as a factor in fat oxidation and call for more research by gender.

sources.title: Sleep in elite athletes and nutritional interventions to enhance sleep
sources.author: Halson SL
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed review in Sports Medicine 44(Suppl 1) by a sport-science recovery researcher.
sources.notes: Reviews why sleep matters for athlete recovery and performance and which dietary factors may influence sleep quality.
sources.population_note: Narrative review mixing men-only, women-only and unreported-sex studies; most athlete samples do not state sex and sex is not analyzed.

sources.title: Running Injury Paradigms and Their Influence on Footwear Design Features and Runner Assessment Methods: A Focused Review to Advance Evidence-Based Practice for Running Medicine Clinicians
sources.author: Agresta C, Giacomazzi C, Harrast M, Zendler J
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed review in Frontiers in Sports and Active Living by running-medicine clinicians and researchers.
sources.notes: Surveys how injury theories such as pronation control, impact and comfort shaped shoe design, and what evidence supports each.
sources.population_note: Cites some female-only and mixed studies (one suggests female, lighter runners keep motion paths less well) but sex is not analyzed and no sex-specific footwear advice.

sources.title: Bone Stress Injuries in Runners Using Carbon Fiber Plate Footwear
sources.author: Tenforde A, Hoenig T, Saxena A, Hollander K
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed article in Sports Medicine by sports-medicine physicians and researchers.
sources.notes: Reports bone stress injuries seen in runners wearing carbon-plated super shoes and discusses possible mechanisms and caution.
sources.population_note: Case series of 5 runners (3 male, 2 female); cases described individually, no RED-S or menstrual discussion; the biomechanics work it relies on used male runners.

sources.title: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition
sources.author: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (ODPHP)
sources.trust_reason: Federal guideline built on the 2018 Physical Activity Guidelines Advisory Committee Scientific Report.
sources.notes: Baseline weekly aerobic and muscle-strengthening targets for adults and the health benefits of activity.
sources.population_note: General adult guidance with a pregnancy and postpartum section; no sex-specific training evidence for athletes.

sources.title: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030
sources.author: U.S. Department of Agriculture and U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
sources.trust_reason: Official federal dietary guidance released by USDA and HHS on 2026-01-07; note this edition skipped the usual advisory-committee process, so pair it with sports-nutrition position stands.
sources.notes: General healthy-eating patterns for the population, emphasizing whole foods and limiting added sugars and highly processed foods.
sources.population_note: General-population guidance with a pregnancy section; sex-specific nutrient tables not confirmed.

sources.title: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance (fact sheet)
sources.author: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
sources.trust_reason: U.S. National Institutes of Health fact sheet, regularly updated.
sources.notes: Ingredient-by-ingredient summary of evidence and safety for supplements marketed for exercise; a health-professional version also exists.
sources.population_note: Fact sheet pages returned 403 and search snippets did not show any sex-related content.

sources.title: Sports and Athletic Performance
sources.author: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics
sources.trust_reason: Consumer pages from the largest professional body of registered dietitian nutritionists in the U.S.
sources.notes: Plain-language articles on eating for exercise at beginner and advanced levels; useful for referring runners to an RDN.

sources.title: Supplement Connect
sources.author: U.S. Anti-Doping Agency (USADA)
sources.trust_reason: Education resource from the national anti-doping organization of the United States.
sources.notes: Explains supplement risks such as contamination and mislabeling and advises third-party certified products (NSF Certified for Sport) if a runner chooses to use them.

sources.title: RRCA Coaching Certification Program
sources.author: Road Runners Club of America
sources.trust_reason: National running organization that runs a long-standing distance-running coach certification with exam and CPR/First Aid requirements.
sources.notes: Describes Level 1 and Level 2 coach certification requirements; useful for vetting a coach's credentials and finding certified coaches.

sources.title: Advanced Marathoning, 4th Edition
sources.author: Pete Pfitzinger and Scott Douglas
sources.trust_reason: Published by Human Kinetics (ISBN 9781718237476); Pfitzinger was the top American finisher in the 1984 and 1988 Olympic marathons.
sources.notes: Marathon training principles plus plans organized by weekly mileage, with tapering and race-day strategy; cite by reference only.

sources.title: Daniels' Running Formula, 4th Edition
sources.author: Jack Daniels
sources.trust_reason: Published by Human Kinetics (ISBN 9781718203662); author created the VDOT training-pace system.
sources.notes: VDOT-based training intensities and plans from 800 m to the marathon; cite by reference only.

sources.title: Run Faster from the 5K to the Marathon: How to Be Your Own Best Coach
sources.author: Brad Hudson and Matt Fitzgerald
sources.trust_reason: Published by Broadway Books/Crown (Penguin Random House, ISBN 9780767928229); Hudson coached elite distance runners.
sources.notes: Adaptive approach to building and adjusting your own plan, with sample programs from 5K to marathon; cite by reference only.

sources.title: 80/20 Running: Run Stronger and Race Faster by Training Slower
sources.author: Matt Fitzgerald
sources.trust_reason: Published by New American Library/Berkley (Penguin, ISBN 9780451470881); author is an established endurance-sports writer.
sources.notes: Makes the case for keeping most running easy and a small share hard, with plans for 5K through marathon; cite by reference only.

sources.title: LA Road Runners Training Resources (ASICS LA Marathon plans, Levels 1-5)
sources.author: LA Road Runners / The McCourt Foundation (Head Coach David Levine)
sources.trust_reason: Published by the LA Marathon's organizer for LA Road Runners, the race's official in-person training program, led by Head Coach David Levine (the site lists no formal credentials).
sources.notes: Free five-level PDF plans of about 25 weeks aimed at the March 2027 race, built around the program's own pace-zone terms.

sources.title: Los Angeles Marathon Distances & Courses
sources.author: The McCourt Foundation
sources.trust_reason: Official course page from the race organizer.
sources.notes: Point-to-point route from Dodger Stadium to Century City with a 7:00am start, 6h30m limit and a downloadable map PDF; no elevation profile in the page text.

sources.title: Boston Marathon Training Plans
sources.author: Boston Athletic Association (B.A.A.)
sources.trust_reason: Plans described as B.A.A.-developed by the race organizer; no individual coach is named.
sources.notes: Four 20-week levels from novice to advanced, from roughly 4 to 7 run days and up to about 60 mi peak weeks; the page forbids reproduction without B.A.A. written consent.

sources.title: 2026 Boston Marathon Course Map (PDF)
sources.author: Boston Athletic Association (B.A.A.)
sources.trust_reason: Official course map PDF linked from the B.A.A. spectator information page.
sources.notes: Point-to-point map from Hopkinton to Boylston Street; B.A.A. has no dedicated HTML course page, so elevation comes from the media guide entry.

sources.title: 130th Boston Marathon Media Guide (PDF)
sources.author: Boston Athletic Association (B.A.A.)
sources.trust_reason: Official B.A.A. media guide whose elevation profile is credited to geographer Sean Hartnett (University of Wisconsin-Eau Claire).
sources.notes: Large PDF with mile-by-mile course elevations, useful for planning downhill-heavy early miles and the Newton hills.

sources.title: TCS New York City Marathon: The Course
sources.author: New York Road Runners (NYRR)
sources.trust_reason: Official course page from the race organizer, New York Road Runners.
sources.notes: Five-borough route with the 2026 course map PDF and the 2026 Bronx change; nyrr.org sends automated fetches to a waiting-room queue, so answer-time fetch may fail.

sources.title: TCS London Marathon: Start Training (training plans)
sources.author: London Marathon Events
sources.trust_reason: Published by the race organizer; the page names no plan author, though third-party sources credit official event coach Martin Yelling.
sources.notes: Free 16-week Beginner, Improver, Advanced and Wheelchair PDF plans for 2026, with Coopah promoted as the official (paid, in-app) training app.

sources.title: TCS London Marathon Course
sources.author: London Marathon Events
sources.trust_reason: Official course page from the race organizer, with section pacing notes from an event pacer.
sources.notes: Mile-by-mile written route from Woolwich to The Mall, noting a net-downhill opening, gentle drop to mile 14 and the rise before Tower Bridge, plus aid station locations.

sources.title: Bank of America Chicago Marathon Training (official Nike plan)
sources.author: Nike, for the Bank of America Chicago Marathon
sources.trust_reason: Hosted by the race organizer as the official plan from Nike; no individual coach is named.
sources.notes: Downloadable 18-week PDF plan (2026 edition) mixing recovery, long, speed and strength sessions with effort-based paces.

sources.title: Bank of America Chicago Marathon Course
sources.author: Bank of America Chicago Marathon
sources.trust_reason: Official course page from the race organizer.
sources.notes: Flat loop through 29 neighborhoods starting and finishing in Grant Park, with a 2026 course map PDF; no elevation or start-time detail on the page.

sources.title: GENERALI BERLIN MARATHON Course
sources.author: SCC EVENTS (Berlin Marathon organizer)
sources.trust_reason: Official course page from the race organizer (the old bmw-berlin-marathon.com URLs now redirect here).
sources.notes: Interactive map still showing the 2026 route, described as the flattest major, elevation listed as tba, with refreshment station kilometers.

sources.title: Tokyo Marathon Course Map
sources.author: Tokyo Marathon Foundation
sources.trust_reason: Official course page from the race organizer.
sources.notes: Route from the Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building to Wadakura Gate with an elevation profile image, map PDF and expected start and passing times for the 2027 race.

sources.title: TCS Sydney Marathon: Marathon course
sources.author: TCS Sydney Marathon (Sydney Marathon organizer)
sources.trust_reason: Official course page from the race organizer.
sources.notes: Hilly route from North Sydney over the Harbour Bridge to the Opera House (+313 m gain), 6:30am mass start, 7-hour cutoff, with an official GPX file and flyover video.

sources.title: Marathon Handbook: Marathon Training Plans
sources.author: Marathon Handbook (plans designed by founder Thomas Watson)
sources.trust_reason: Plans credited to founder Thomas Watson, self-described UESCA-certified running coach and ultrarunner, and marked as reviewed by an unnamed in-house coaching team.
sources.notes: Free index of beginner through advanced and sub-4, sub-3:30 and sub-3 plans of 8 to 26 weeks; the site is affiliate-funded and sells paid TrainingPeaks versions.

sources.title: Venice Run Club: Marathon Training
sources.author: Venice Run Club (founded by Justin and Tyler)
sources.trust_reason: Community run club page; no coaches or coaching credentials are named anywhere on the site.
sources.notes: Free Level I-III marathon plans hosted as Google Drive and Sheets files, alongside free group runs in Venice, CA; treat as low-authority community material.

sources.title: Hal Higdon: Marathon Training for All Skill Levels
sources.author: Hal Higdon
sources.trust_reason: Written by Hal Higdon, longtime Runner's World contributing editor, RRCA co-founder and author of Marathon: The Ultimate Training Guide; no coaching certification is claimed.
sources.notes: Widely used free library of mostly 18-week plans from Novice 1 to Advanced 2 plus longer and specialty variants, with paid interactive versions on TrainingPeaks.

sources.title: International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutritional concerns of the female athlete
sources.author: Sims ST, Kerksick CM, Smith-Ryan AE, Janse de Jonge XAK, et al. (International Society of Sports Nutrition)
sources.trust_reason: Official ISSN position stand, peer reviewed, J Int Soc Sports Nutr 20(1):2204066.
sources.notes: Covers energy availability, carbohydrate and protein needs across menstrual cycle phases, contraceptive use and menopause, and suggests women track their own hormonal status against training and recovery.
sources.population_note: Expert review of literature on female athletes of reproductive age through peri- and post-menopause; no single study sample.

sources.title: Sex differences and considerations for female specific nutritional strategies: a narrative review
sources.author: Wohlgemuth KJ, Arieta LR, Brewer GJ, Hoselton AL, Gould LM, Smith-Ryan AE
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed narrative review in J Int Soc Sports Nutr 18:27.
sources.notes: Practical summary of how hormonal changes across the cycle and lifespan shift nutrition and supplement considerations for active women.
sources.population_note: Narrative synthesis of literature on active females and female athletes; no pooled sample.

sources.title: Protein Requirements of Pre-Menopausal Female Athletes: Systematic Literature Review
sources.author: Mercer D, Convit L, Condo D, Carr AJ, Hamilton DL, Slater G, Snipe RMJ
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed systematic review in Nutrients 12(11):3527, quality graded with the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics checklist.
sources.notes: Estimates daily protein needs for premenopausal women doing endurance, resistance and intermittent exercise, and finds too little data to say whether cycle phase or contraception changes them.
sources.population_note: 14 studies, 204 recreationally active or competitive premenopausal women (about 18-45 years).

sources.title: The Effects of Menstrual Cycle Phase on Exercise Performance in Eumenorrheic Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.author: McNulty KL, Elliott-Sale KJ, Dolan E, Swinton PA, Ansdell P, Goodall S, Thomas K, Hicks KM
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis in Sports Med 50(10):1813-1827, GRADE-based quality assessment.
sources.notes: Finds performance may be trivially lower in the early follicular phase, but evidence is mostly low quality and varied, so it favors individual tracking over blanket cycle-based rules.
sources.population_note: 78 studies, 1,193 naturally menstruating women; 51 studies (709 women) in the pairwise meta-analysis.

sources.title: The Effects of Oral Contraceptives on Exercise Performance in Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
sources.author: Elliott-Sale KJ, McNulty KL, Ansdell P, Goodall S, Hicks KM, Thomas K, Swinton PA, Dolan E
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis in Sports Med 50(10):1785-1812.
sources.notes: Compares pill users with naturally menstruating women and pill-taking days with withdrawal days, finding at most small performance differences and mostly low-quality evidence.
sources.population_note: 42 studies, 590 women (oral contraceptive users and naturally menstruating comparators).

sources.title: Methodological Considerations for Studies in Sport and Exercise Science with Women as Participants: A Working Guide for Standards of Practice for Research on Women
sources.author: Elliott-Sale KJ, Minahan CL, de Jonge XAKJ, Ackerman KE, Sipila S, Constantini NW, Lebrun CM, Hackney AC
sources.trust_reason: Expert methodological statement, peer reviewed, Sports Med 51(5):843-861.
sources.notes: Sets standards for classifying menstrual status, contraceptive use, pregnancy and menopause in studies, which helps the coach judge how well a study's findings apply to women.
sources.population_note: Methods guidance for research with women from non-athletes to athletes; no study sample.

sources.title: "Invisible Sportswomen": The Sex Data Gap in Sport and Exercise Science Research
sources.author: Cowley ES, Olenick AA, McNulty KL, Ross EZ
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed audit in Women in Sport and Physical Activity Journal 29(2):146-151 (Human Kinetics).
sources.notes: Audits who was studied in six sport science journals and shows women are a minority of participants and rarely studied alone, a reason to flag male-only evidence.
sources.population_note: 5,261 papers from 6 journals (2014-2020), 12.5 million participants: 34% female; 6% of papers studied females only.

sources.title: Iron deficiency, supplementation, and sports performance in female athletes: A systematic review
sources.author: Pengelly M, Pumpa K, Pyne DB, Etxebarria N
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed systematic review in J Sport Health Sci 14:101009, quality assessed with a modified Downs and Black checklist.
sources.notes: Links iron deficiency to a small drop in endurance performance in trained women and reports gains after medically supervised supplementation; useful context for advising a blood test with a doctor.
sources.population_note: 23 studies, 669 high-level female athletes aged 13-47 across 16 sports, iron deficient defined as serum ferritin under 40 ug/L.

sources.title: Factors Associated With High-Risk and Low-Risk Bone Stress Injury in Female Runners: Implications for Risk Factor Stratification and Management
sources.author: Tenforde AS, Ackerman KE, Bouxsein ML, Gaudette L, et al., Popp KL
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed cross-sectional study in Orthop J Sports Med 12(5).
sources.notes: Compares women with high-risk (pelvis, femoral neck) versus low-risk (shin, foot) bone stress injuries on bone density, menstrual history, eating behavior and running load rates.
sources.population_note: 45 premenopausal women runners: 15 with high-risk BSI history, 15 with low-risk BSI history, 15 with none.

sources.title: 2025 Update to the Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement Part 2: Clinical Guidelines for Screening, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Return to Play for Adolescents and Adults
sources.author: Williams NI, De Souza MJ, Misra M, Nattiv A, Joy E, Barrack M, et al. (Female Athlete Triad Coalition)
sources.trust_reason: Consensus statement of the Female Athlete Triad Coalition, peer reviewed, Sports Med 56(2):375-427; updates the 2014 consensus.
sources.notes: Updates screening, treatment and return-to-play guidance for low energy, menstrual disturbance and bone loss, now counting bone stress injuries in the bone spectrum and moving away from a single energy availability cutoff.
sources.population_note: Expert consensus on adolescent and adult female athletes; no single study sample.

sources.title: Heat Adaptation for Females: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Physiological Adaptations and Exercise Performance in the Heat
sources.author: Kelly MK, Bowe SJ, Jardine WT, Condo D, Guy JH, Snow RJ, Carr AJ
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed systematic review and meta-analysis in Sports Med 53(7):1395-1421.
sources.notes: Shows heat training lowers core temperature and heart rate and raises sweat rate in women and improves performance in the heat, with notes on the exposure doses that worked best.
sources.population_note: 30 studies (22 meta-analysed), 235 women completing heat training; most studies did not control cycle phase.

sources.title: Sex-Specific Differences in Running Injuries: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression
sources.author: Hollander K, Rahlf AL, Wilke J, Edler C, Steib S, Junge A, Zech A
sources.trust_reason: Peer-reviewed systematic review and meta-analysis in Sports Med 51(5):1011-1039, PRISMA methods.
sources.notes: Finds similar overall injury rates in women and men but a roughly doubled bone stress injury risk in women, while men get more Achilles problems.
sources.population_note: 38 prospective studies; injury data from 35,689 runners, 40.8% female.

sources.title: Returning to running postnatal: guidelines for medical, health and fitness professionals managing this population
sources.author: Goom T, Donnelly G, Brockwell E
sources.trust_reason: Clinician guideline written by a sports physiotherapist and two pelvic health physiotherapists after expert feedback; later summarized as a BJSM infographic (2020).
sources.notes: Lists pelvic floor and abdominal checks, risk factors and graded strength and impact readiness tests before running after childbirth; the coach uses it only as context when referring to a pelvic health physio.
sources.population_note: Clinical guidance for postnatal women returning to running; not a study sample.

sources.title: ROAR, Revised Edition: Match Your Food and Fitness to Your Unique Female Physiology
sources.author: Sims ST
sources.trust_reason: Book by an exercise physiologist and nutrition scientist, published by Rodale/Harmony (Penguin Random House), ISBN 9780593581926; revision of the 2016 Rodale original.
sources.notes: Popular, research-informed guide to training and eating around the menstrual cycle and menopause; cite by reference only and prefer the peer-reviewed sources for specific numbers.
sources.population_note: Written for active women across the lifespan; not a study.

sources.title: Athletic Records and Human Endurance
sources.author: Riegel PS
sources.trust_reason: Published in American Scientist 69(3):285-290 (Sigma Xi); origin of the widely used Riegel race-time prediction formula.
sources.notes: Fits a time-versus-distance power law to world-record performances; basis of T2 = T1 * (D2/D1)^1.06 used by `coach pace`. JSTOR page, so cite and link only.
sources.population_note: Fit to elite world-record performances, not recreational runners. Full text not reviewed, so how much women's records shaped the 1.06 exponent is unconfirmed; not validated separately for women.
